definition: Myriad means consisting of a very great number — so many that counting them is hopeless.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word myriad. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know myriad should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: From the ferry's top deck the harbor's myriad lights ran together into one glowing smear, past any hope of counting.
Numerous is weaker than myriad: numerous complaints can still be logged and tallied one by one, while myriad complaints have outrun the tally entirely.
Infinite goes further than myriad — myriad things merely defeat the counting, but infinite things have no end at all, no matter how long the count runs.

Countless says flatly that counting is impossible — it is the everyday, plain-spoken twin. Myriad says the same thing in a higher register and often adds a shimmer of variety: myriad lights, myriad voices.

Innumerable, like myriad, means too many to number, but it stays an ordinary adjective for bulk. Myriad carries its Greek history — the ten-thousand — and a literary flavor, which is why poems reach for myriad and reports for innumerable.

Myriad means consisting of a very great number — so many that counting them is hopeless.
Open the hive and the myriad workers stop being individual bees at all: thirty, forty, fifty thousand bodies moving as one shimmering skin over the comb.
Myriad does the work 'many' can't: it asserts a number so great that counting stops being worth attempting.
Fifty thousand bees aren't merely numerous — the tally collapses into a single shimmering impression, and myriad is the word for that.
Myriad asserts number, not just variety: it says the count has outrun anyone's patience to finish it.
A list you can actually complete — however varied — is numerous or assorted, not myriad.
Both constructions are standard, and have been for centuries: 'myriad stars' and 'a myriad of stars' are equally good English.

The museum's entomology wing keeps its treasures in shallow drawers, four hundred of them, stacked floor to ceiling.
Slide one open and the first impression is not order but abundance: beetles in myriad forms -- metallic green, horned, flat as seeds, some smaller than the pins that hold them.
The collection began with a Victorian curate's shoebox and now holds more specimens than the museum has ever fully cataloged.
Curators estimate the backlog at two million entries, and the estimate itself is a decade old.
Visiting students are handed a single drawer and a magnifier -- a manageable slice of a variety that resists any complete accounting.
